extracted.intended_audience: electric cooperative leaders, grid operators, policymakers, and energy-sector stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate near-term (seasonal) and longer-term electric grid reliability risks, the metrics that drive those risks, and policy/operational responses that co-ops and policymakers should pursue. Emphasis on summer resource adequacy, changing resource mix, and legislative priorities that affect reliability and affordability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summer resource and transmission adequacy (NERC 2025 Summer Reliability Assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: NERC evaluated generation resource and transmission system adequacy for June through September and warned of potential energy supply shortfalls in parts of the U.S. this summer during periods of extreme weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All areas studied are expected to have adequate resources for normal summer peak load conditions, but several regions (New England, parts of the Midwest, the Southwest Power Pool and Texas) are at risk of supply shortfalls during more extreme summer weather. Consider regional weather forecasts (above-average temperatures, below-average precipitation), and stress scenarios beyond 'normal peak' when judging adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish normal peak adequacy vs. extreme-weather risk
rubrics_metrics.description: All areas may be adequate for normal peak loads yet still face shortfalls under extreme conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliability assessments should explicitly model both 'normal summer peak' and extreme weather/planning scenarios; identify regions that are adequate under base case but vulnerable under stress cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity and demand change metrics (quantitative indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track changes in peak electricity demand, retired/inactive generator capacity, and new on-peak capacity additions (solar, battery, wind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hard metrics to quantify risk: the report cites >10 GW increase in peak demand since last summer, >7.4 GW of retired/inactive capacity (mostly gas and coal), and over 40 GW of on-peak capacity gains from solar, battery and wind. Evaluate net effect on reserve margins, timing of additions, and whether added capacity provides the needed services at peak times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource-mix flexibility and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: The changing resource mix (more solar, batteries, wind; fewer thermal plants) is generally less flexible and more variable, creating operational challenges to meet higher demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess resources not only by nameplate capacity but by flexibility, ramping capability, dispatchability and variability. Consider 'pace and performance of buildout'—whether new resources come online in the right locations and with performance characteristics aligned with reliability needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator preparedness and conservative operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmission owners and grid authorities should review operating plans and operate conservatively to ensure adequate resource availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guidance from NERC: review and update plans, prepare conservative operating strategies during stressed conditions, and ensure reserve and contingency procedures are in place to maintain service during shortages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparedness for inverter-based resource tripping
rubrics_metrics.description: Grid operators should be prepared for the potential of inverter-based resources (solar PV and batteries) to unexpectedly trip during grid disturbances (e.g., short circuits or line breaks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliability planning should include contingencies for sudden loss of inverter-based capacity, protection settings, ride-through behavior, and coordination of inverter control strategies with system protection schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand response as an emergency load-reduction tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracted demand response resources can reduce loads if demand hits record levels and available generation is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the availability and contractual readiness of demand response programs as a load-shedding or emergency resource. PJM indicated reliance on contracted demand response as a potential measure to reduce loads under extreme demand scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term capacity adequacy and retirement risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-Term Reliability Assessment projects that over half of North America is at risk of energy shortfalls in the next 10 years due to surging demand and thermal plant retirements; capacity additions are projected to fall short of demand growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term planning should account for retirement schedules, projected demand growth (electrification, data centers, industrialization), and realistic timelines for replacement capacity. Use long-range models to identify where capacity additions will be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting reform as a policy criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing permitting reform to shorten federal approval timelines and provide predictability is a top legislative priority to enable timely construction of electric infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate permitting reforms on whether they provide shorter timelines, greater predictability, and judicial reform to limit delay lawsuits, while maintaining environmental and public health protections. Policymakers should balance speed and certainty without weakening protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose regulatory changes that force premature plant closures (EPA power plant rule concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: NRECA argues the EPA power plant rule jeopardizes grid reliability by forcing premature closure of coal-fired plants, imposing unworkable emissions reductions on new natural gas plants, and mandating unproven technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy assessments should weigh reliability impacts of emissions rules, considering whether compliance costs or technological mandates would materially reduce the operation of dispatchable resources needed for reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect hydropower as a reliability resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect hydropower resources (e.g., oppose breaching of Lower Snake River dams) because they provide reliable, abundant, carbon-free power underpinning regional reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating policy actions affecting hydro assets, include the reliability value of firm, dispatchable, carbon-free generation in regional adequacy assessments and cost-benefit analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend against wildfires by expediting hazardous-tree removal permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it easier for co-ops to remove hazardous trees on federal land that could fall onto electric lines and spark wildfires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and permitting processes should be judged by their ability to expedite vegetation management permitting to reduce wildfire risk to distribution and transmission lines. Consider administrative fixes (e.g., Fix Our Forests Act) to reduce permit backlogs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support funding for Rural Utilities Service (RUS) Electric Loans
rubrics_metrics.description: Full funding for the RUS Electric Loan program is a co-op priority; the program finances construction of electric infrastructure in rural communities and is repaid with interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate federal budget and program support by whether it ensures rural co-ops can finance infrastructure, modernize systems, and maintain reliability and affordability for member-consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combustion turbine (CT) regulatory impact and cost-effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: CTs are essential, versatile dispatchable units; proposed EPA controls may substantially underestimate compliance costs and could arbitrarily limit CT operation, harming reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory reviews should assess the cost-effectiveness of required emissions-control technologies for CTs, the operational role of CTs (quick start, ramping, grid stabilization), and whether rule changes would inappropriately constrain units that support reliability and renewable integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to elective-pay tax credits for co-op project viability
rubrics_metrics.description: Elective-pay tax credits (direct payment option) enable co-ops and tax-exempt entities to access investment tax credits, lowering project costs and enabling co-ops to build, own and operate eligible generation and storage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging project financial viability, include availability of elective-pay credits and the ability to stack credits with grants/loans. The page cites elective-pay reducing project costs by >20% and enabling projects that otherwise would not be financially viable for co-ops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize always-available, dispatchable generation in resource portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: A diverse portfolio anchored by always-available, dispatchable generation is essential to meet skyrocketing electricity demand and ensure reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource planning and policy should prioritize dispatchable resources that can run when needed. Assess portfolios by contribution to reliability (capacity value, availability during extremes), not just by aggregate renewable capacity.
